_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: Brownsville let SpaceX's land go in August. Starbase now hears a tax abatement for a gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility there on December 9th.

introduction.text: [The City of Starbase has given notice that its City Commission will meet in public session on {{date:c4}} at 48491 State Highway 4](c4). [The commission will consider a property tax abatement under Chapter {{number:c5}} of the Texas Tax Code and a related economic development agreement under Chapter {{number:c5:1}} of the Local Government Code](c5). [The applicant and property owner is Space Exploration Technologies Corp.](c6)

[The notice describes a gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility that SpaceX proposes to construct, own and operate](c1). [It estimates capital investment for the initial phases at approximately {{money:c2}}, built in multiple phases with possible future expansions](c2). [The public is invited to attend and be heard](c7).

paragraphs.text: [The notice places the site inside Starbase's corporate limits, on an approximately {{number:c3}} acre tract just east of Brownsville between Boca Chica Blvd and the Port of Brownsville](c3). [It says the project would sit in the Cameron County Enterprise Zone, which it treats as a reinvestment zone for the abatement](c8).

[The Texas Tribune reported on {{date:c14}} that Brownsville commissioners voted unanimously at a weekend special meeting to de-annex the land](c14). [SpaceX agreed in exchange to give Brownsville up to {{money:c15}} for water and wastewater projects, the Tribune reported](c15). [Sheila McCorkle, a SpaceX vice president, told commissioners the company sought de-annexation because the city provided no services to the area](c20), [and she said the deal would be off the table unless it was approved that day](c16). [Starbase later annexed the land](c10).

[A Brownsville resident, Uriel Gavito, asked at the meeting why the city was rushing and why it was meeting on a Saturday](c21). [Brownsville said in a statement that it stood by the decision, based on the information and circumstances presented at the time](c17).

sections.heading: A pause the tract sits outside

paragraphs.text: [The Tribune reported on {{date:c13}} that Brownsville's {{number:c13}} day moratorium on data center applications in the city and its extraterritorial jurisdiction had taken effect the week before](c13). [Its account says the SpaceX project circumvents that moratorium](c9). The notice itself does not mention the moratorium, and Brownsville's own page on it refused an automated fetch, so this account rests on the Tribune.

[The Tribune reports the planned gas-fired plant could power the data center so that it avoids connecting to the state grid](c11). [It also reports that Governor Greg Abbott directed grid operators in August to pause data center connection requests until the data centers could be audited](c18), [and that some data centers could still go ahead by supplying their own electricity](c19). Whether this site will connect to ERCOT is not established by any document in this record.

sections.heading: What the December hearing decides, and what is still missing

paragraphs.text: [The commission meets to consider the agreements](c5). Nothing has been approved. No plat, site plan, turbine count, water demand or building design appears in the notice. [SpaceX did not answer the Tribune's questions about the project](c12).

[The South Texas Environmental Justice Network announced a protest and argued the facilities would pollute the air, use up water and raise residents' energy bills](c22). [A Brownsville teacher, Janie Melendez, told the Tribune many people in the community need jobs and that SpaceX has contributed to those jobs](c23).
